skills.name: Inflation: causes, effects and policy choices

note.text: Demand-pull pressure can arise when spending grows faster than productive capacity. Cost-push pressure can arise from higher input costs or disrupted supply. Expectations can influence wage and price decisions. These mechanisms may interact; one example does not identify every cause. Unanticipated inflation can reduce the real value of fixed nominal balances and change the real burden of fixed nominal debts. Outcomes depend on income adjustment, contract terms and policy response. Measures restraining demand can have output costs and do not directly repair every supply disruption.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to connect a stated inflation pressure to a mechanism and explain a conditional effect. Builds on: price-index changes and nominal versus real value. Leads to: deflation and central-bank policy.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: In a fictional case, transport disruption raises costs across several producers while another case describes spending pressing against limited capacity. The first illustrates a supply pressure; the second a demand pressure. A household’s unchanged nominal cash balance buys less if its relevant basket costs more. No current inflation forecast or investment choice is supplied.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Name the stated change, trace a plausible mechanism and qualify the conclusion. Separate a nominal amount from its real purchasing ability. Match a proposed policy to the pressure, recognising time lags and trade-offs rather than promising an immediate cure.

key_words.meaning: spending growth pressing beyond available productive capacity
upward price pressure from higher costs or supply disruption
a change in purchasing ability despite a fixed nominal amount
a policy benefit considered with costs and limits

mistake.wrong: Any demand increase must cause the same inflation whatever unused capacity exists.
mistake.right: demand-pull pressure: spending growth pressing beyond available productive capacity.
mistake.why: Capacity and supply response affect the outcome.

cards.idea: Distinguish the monetary concepts before evaluating a case.
example: demand-pull pressure: spending growth pressing beyond available productive capacity.
cost-push pressure: upward price pressure from higher costs or supply disruption.
real-value effect: a change in purchasing ability despite a fixed nominal amount.
policy trade-off: a policy benefit considered with costs and limits.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: Broad spending rises while output capacity cannot keep pace.
Transport disruption raises input costs across producers.
Unchanged cash covers less of a more expensive basket.
Demand restraint may reduce pressure while slowing activity.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.
example: demand-pull pressure: Capacity and supply response affect the outcome.
cost-push pressure: It can reduce availability or raise costs instead.
real-value effect: Prices affect purchasing ability.
policy trade-off: Mechanisms, delays and side effects matter.

w: It proves every borrower benefits equally.

pick.r: It can restrain spending while also slowing activity.
w: It directly restores every damaged supply route.
e: Demand restraint is not physical route repair.
Policy effects can take time.
Output costs are possible.
pick.y: Match the mechanism and its limits.
